buildStartedMarker.note: build_site.py makes `pending` afresh the moment a build begins, before it reads the settings or any page, and renames it to `file` only once that build's site has been copied out — so `file` always describes the site that is there, and a build that fails, is stopped, or is a preview leaves it alone. The TIME of the file is the start time; nothing is written into it that anything reads. Measured on Colima 2026-09-24: a file made from inside the container is stamped by the host's clock, the one the teacher's Save is stamped with, so no clocks are compared. Both names begin with a dot so the freshness checks, which skip hidden entries, never count them as content, and nothing outside public/ is published. Read by BuildFreshness in each app and by the scheduled publish's own check, which must agree.
buildStartedMarker.where: Beside the section's built site: .merged_output/section<N>/, the folder that holds public/.

buildFreshness.note: Whether a deploy has to build first. Getting this wrong in one direction wastes minutes; in the other it publishes yesterday's site.

previewBuild.note: One rule for 'this built site is a preview's', read by every checker: BuildFreshness in each app, the mac's scheduled publish (its own shell check, because the app is closed when it runs), deploy.sh (three times), deploy.py and deploy.ps1. Serve mode bakes the live-reload client into EVERY page and the built tree is replaced file by file, so a clean front page in front of a preview's pages is a real state — deploy.sh found it on 2026-09-05 and has read the whole tree since, as has deploy.py. The apps read the front page alone until issue #136: they called that state deploy-fresh, skipped their build, and the LAUNCHER then rebuilt under the destination's leg — the build's milestones missing from the panel, and on the mac a question the build asked overnight reported as the destination's. A reader narrower than the launchers is the fault, whichever side it is on. Each case is a tree under the section's public/ folder; `unreadable` names pages that exist but cannot be opened.
previewBuild.notShared: Three things are deliberately NOT cases. (1) A front page that is MISSING or cannot be READ: the apps rebuild (`rules` → 'the built index cannot be read'), while the launchers stop at the copy instead — a different rule, pinned where it lives. (2) A page that is not valid UTF-8: measured 2026-09-25 on macOS 26.6, /usr/bin/grep 2.6.0-FreeBSD under a UTF-8 locale does NOT find the signature on a line that also holds an invalid byte (exit 1), and under LC_ALL=C it does (exit 0), so deploy.sh run from a Terminal can call such a page clean while the apps (bytes), the scheduled check (LC_ALL=C) and deploy.py (errors='ignore') call it a preview's. The error is in the SAFE direction — the app rebuilds first — and Quartz only writes UTF-8, so it is written down rather than pinned. (3) Upper-case .HTML, and a public/ that is ITSELF a symbolic link (neither FileManager's enumerator nor grep -r descends into one; a link further up, such as the mac's .merged_output, is followed by both — measured): Quartz produces neither. deploy.ps1 also matches the signature without regard to case (Select-String's default), which no case here can tell apart.
previewBuild.where: Every file whose name ends .html anywhere under the section's built public/ folder, hidden folders included, compared as bytes; the front page first, so a real preview's build answers from one file. A page that cannot be opened is passed over, as every launcher does.

rules.when: the built site is older than the teacher's newest content
the built site was made by a PREVIEW
rules.why: **The one that is not obvious.** Serve mode bakes a live-reload client pointed at ws://localhost into every page. Publishing that makes visitors' browsers ask about 'access to other apps and services on this device' — so a preview build is never deploy-fresh, however recent it is. Detected by ANY built page containing the signature — `previewBuild`, which every checker reads (issue #136; the front page alone until then).

rules.when: the built site is newer than the content and was not built by a preview
the built index cannot be read
something was saved AFTER the build that made the site started, even though the built site is newer
rules.why: Issue #265. A build reads the settings and the pages when it starts and writes index.html minutes later, so a Save made while a publish was building is OLDER than index.html. Compared with index.html alone it looked built: the next Publish sent the same old site, said it had succeeded, and settingsSavedWhilePublishing told the teacher to do exactly that. So the time compared with is the START of the build that made the site on disk — read from buildStartedMarker when it is there, and the earlier of it and index.html's time when both are (an earlier time only ever costs a rebuild that was not needed; a later one sends a stale site). With no marker (a site built before this existed) index.html's time is used, as before. Rejected: comparing the build's copy of course_config.json with the course's (the plan review's A3) — the build copies the settings some seconds AFTER it reads them, so a Save in between matches the copy and is still missed, and it would not catch a PAGE saved during the build, which this does.

buildFreshness.theLaunchersMustDoThisToo: These rules were implemented in the APPS only, and that left a hole for two years' worth of command-line use. `deploy.py` refuses a preview build for the Netlify and Cloudflare destinations, but publishing TO A FOLDER is handled entirely host-side by `deploy.sh` / `deploy.ps1` — it never enters the container, so `deploy.py` never runs. From the command line, `./preview.sh CODE N` followed by `./deploy.sh CODE N --to-folder …` therefore published the live-reload client: measured 2026-09-05 as 230 of 244 files. The apps were never exposed, because BuildFreshness forces a rebuild first, which is why three destinations tested clean in August. That held for a whole preview's build, whose front page carries the client too; the MIXED state in (1) below reached the apps until issue #136, because they read the front page alone. They now read the same tree as the launchers — `previewBuild`. Both launchers now make the same check and rebuild. THREE things are needed, and each was discovered by getting it wrong. (1) The CHECK must read every HTML page, not just index.html: serve mode bakes the client into all of them and the tree is replaced file by file, so a clean front page in front of stale preview pages is a real state that front-page detection cannot see and publishes untouched. (2) The rebuild must STOP a preview that is still serving that section: the preview's sync watcher mirrors the serve build to the host every second and overwrites the rebuild within a second of it finishing. This was first blamed on bind-mount lag, which was wrong — a rebuild takes about 3 seconds and the tree is clean the moment it returns; the cause was always the race. (3) The WAIT after the rebuild must also cover every HTML page, for the same reason as (1).

credentialPrompts.expiryAdviceIsLoadBearing: Both token steps tell the teacher to set an expiry past the end of the school year. deployArguments.note: Given a course's configuration, what deploy.sh is asked to do. One place must decide this in each app — on the mac it is DeployCommand.arguments, shared by the Deploy button, the assistant and the scheduled-deploy alarm. Built separately anywhere and this happens: the assistant path never passed --target cloudflare, and a Cloudflare course deployed to Netlify. Nothing failed; the site simply appeared on the wrong host. Netlify passes NO target flag at all — it is the launcher's default, and every course written before Cloudflare existed relies on that. A course can configure more than one destination now (additional_deploy_targets, in file-formats.json) — Deploy walks them in order and calls this same argument-building logic once per destination, so every case above still applies per leg; there is no separate multi-destination argument shape to test. A case may carry `unattended: true`, which is what the SCHEDULED deploy passes and nothing else does — the Deploy button, the assistant and an MCP client all leave it off. It adds `--non-interactive`, which tells the launcher that any question a teacher would have to answer must become a refusal rather than a prompt nobody can answer or a default nobody chose. What it refuses, on both platforms, is launcherFlags.nonInteractive.

Matched NARROWLY, on "bind source path does not exist" and nothing wider: "Error response from daemon" was the tempting substring and would have said this to a teacher whose disk was full or whose engine had restarted mid-run. THE COMMONEST CAUSE IS A FOLDER THE BUILDER CANNOT REACH, which is why the sentence names the home folder. Measured 2026-09-19 on macOS/virtiofs, with paths the virtual machine had never been handed, three of three, plus /Users/Shared: a working folder outside the home folder is REFUSED with this output. It was not refused before — the older `-v` form created the folder inside the virtual machine and started, so the build ran against an EMPTY folder, reported success and produced nothing, and an earlier measurement that said both forms behaved alike had been contaminated by running `-v` first on the same path. Saying "keep it in your home folder" is honest now because something finally enforces it. Two rarer causes share this output and are knowingly not named in the sentence: a folder that moved between the launcher's own check and the moment the workspace is made, and a builds folder that could not be created at all because the disk is full or Application Support cannot be written to. The launchers say the SAME sentence themselves, for a teacher at the command line and for a publish launchd ran overnight, and scripts/test_container_mount.sh checks their copy against this one. A SECOND launcher sentence, for a working folder that is simply not there any more, has no case here on purpose: that check happens before anything is asked of the builder, so there is no output for the app to recognise. Until 2026-09-19 a colon in the folder's name was the commonest cause of all — a teacher typing "Comm Tech 26/27" in Finder gets "Comm Tech 26:27" on disk — and the launchers now handle that (GitHub issue #221).

alsoAccepted.note: Preview flags the launchers accept that the apps do not currently pass. Listed so nobody removes one on the assumption it is dead, and so a new app feature knows what is already there.

deployExtras.asymmetry: deploy.sh looks for this flag TWICE — once in a pre-scan before its 'Open' course-code guard, which asks a question before the flag loop runs, and once in the loop itself. deploy.ps1 needs no pre-scan: it parses its flags first and asks afterwards.
deployExtras.meaning: Refuse rather than ask. Every question this publish could put to a teacher is answered by stopping, saying which question it was, and exiting 3.
usedFor: a publish set to happen on its own
deployExtras.why: A scheduled publish runs at half six with the app closed, so every question is one NOBODY will answer, and both ways that ended have been seen. With a terminal, deploy.py's `input()` BLOCKS — measured at 45 minutes, the launcher and its Python child still waiting when they were swept up, and the teacher's site simply not updated in the morning with nothing said. Without one, `prompt()` returns its DEFAULT silently and a Netlify name conflict auto-suffixes, so the site is published to an address nobody chose. Exit code 3 means "a question went unanswered" and nothing else, so a caller can tell it from an ordinary failure and say something true to the teacher; every other exit in deploy.py and in both launchers is 0 or 1. PASSED BY THE SCHEDULED WRAPPER, never by the app's Deploy button — whether anybody is there to answer is a fact about who is RUNNING, not about the course, which is why it is not in `deployArguments`. Parsing it is not enough: both launchers must FORWARD it to deploy.py, where the site-name question lives.

deployExtras.meaning: Print what the deploy would do and why it thinks so.
deployExtras.why: A support tool, run by hand when a teacher's deploy misbehaves.

deployExtras.meaning: Publish using a particular already-built image instead of the one the recipe hashes to.
deployExtras.why: NOT shared, recorded 2026-09-06 when this list was first run against the launchers. `deploy.sh` parses it; `deploy.ps1` does not, and cannot — Windows dropped Docker for a native runtime on 2026-08-19 (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md entry 290), so there is no image for a tag to name. The right answer was to write the divergence down rather than add a flag that does nothing to a launcher so a test would pass. `--diagnose` above IS shared and both launchers take it.

deployExtras.meaning: Nobody is at the computer. Anything that would stop and ask — a Netlify or Cloudflare credential, a name for a website that does not exist yet — stops the publish instead, saying which question it could not ask.
usedFor: a scheduled publish, which runs at a time the teacher chose and then went to bed for
deployExtras.why: Both alternatives were seen for real (TODO.md, 2026-09-06). With a terminal on standard input, deploy.py's input() WAITS — two measured runs sat at one prompt for 45 minutes — and the teacher's site is simply not updated in the morning, with nothing to say why. Without one, sys.stdin.isatty() is false and the DEFAULT is taken silently, so the site is published at an address nobody chose. Refusing is the only answer that neither hangs nor publishes something unasked for. The launcher passes the same flag on to deploy.py, and asks for no terminal at all when it is set, so the waiting branch cannot exist.

nonInteractive.note: What `--non-interactive` must refuse, on BOTH platforms. The list is the point: a flag that refuses in six places on one platform and four on the other is a scheduled publish that hangs on one of them. deploy.py is shared Python, so those refusals cannot drift; the launcher's own are per-platform and are written out here so the second one is copied rather than invented. The course-code guard is refused as of 2026-09-09; it is the FIRST entry below, and the entry carries what was rejected and why.

refusals.bothLaunchers: deploy.sh AND preview.sh, and the second is the one that is easy to miss. A scheduled publish BUILDS before it publishes, and the mac's launchd agent runs preview.sh --build-only directly. preview.sh has no `set -e`, so without the flag its read fails at end of input, `${_ans:-Y}` takes the DEFAULT, and the build retargets a DIFFERENT course code — which then publishes successfully against the wrong course. That is a worse failure than a refusal, because nothing looks wrong.
refusals.question: Fix course code to '<CODE>'? [Y/n] — the guard for a code ending in a digit zero
refusals.reachedWhen: The course code matches three letters, a digit and a zero. DECIDED by Russell 2026-09-09 to refuse; it was deliberately unchanged before that, and the reasoning both ways is kept below because it was measured rather than guessed.
refusals.refuse: Say which question could not be asked, and that publishing or previewing this section once from Plantoir sorts it out.
refusals.rejected: KEEPING THE CODE AS TYPED, which was the other defensible answer and is recorded so it is not re-proposed as new: by the time a schedule exists the code came from course_config.json rather than a keyboard, so there is no typo to fix, and a genuinely wrong code still fails loudly at "Course folder not found". It was rejected because a silent retarget on the build leg is indistinguishable from success, and because a refusal that names the question is consistent with every other question under this flag. The cost is real and worth stating: a teacher whose course code is hand-typed in that shape — ENG10, MAT10 — cannot publish unattended until the code is changed.
refusals.whatHappenedBefore: TWO different unattended failures, one per launcher, and a scheduled publish meets both because it builds before it publishes. `preview.sh` has no `set -e`: the read fails at end of input, the answer variable stays empty, the [Y/n] DEFAULT is taken, and the build retargets a DIFFERENT course code — announcing it with “Using corrected course code”, which nobody is there to read. `deploy.sh` has `set -euo pipefail`: the same failed read ends the script on the spot with exit 1. Measured: it prints the guard's two explanatory lines (“It looks like you entered 'ICS30'…”) and then stops — no prompt text, no error, no reason. So the shape today is “builds the wrong course, then stops mid-sentence”.
refusals.whoItReaches: MEASURED 2026-09-06, and it is narrower than the first draft of this entry claimed. The guard matches three letters, a digit and a zero — and NO code in either catalogue the wizard offers matches it: 0 of 1930 Ontario codes and 0 of 117 British Columbia codes (BC codes are MFMP-10 / MPREC11 shaped). A course code is free text up to twelve characters (CourseCodeRule), so it is still reachable — but only by a code a teacher typed freehand, which is exactly the case the guard was written for. That cuts BOTH ways in the decision below: refusing breaks far fewer real courses than feared, and the whole prompt is rarer than it looks.

refusals.question: Continue anyway? [y/N] — the warning when a section is not listed in course_config.json
refusals.reachedWhen: preview.ps1 is asked to build a section the course's configuration does not list. WINDOWS ONLY, and not drift: preview.sh has exactly one read prompt (its course-code guard) and simply does not ask this. Added from Windows 2026-09-09; launcherFlags is authored rather than generated, so that side could record it without asking the mac.
refusals.refuse: Say which question could not be asked, and that adding this section to the course in Plantoir — or previewing it once by hand — answers it.
refusals.whatHappenedBefore: Its default is NO, so an unattended build of an unlisted section printed "Cancelled." and exited 1 to a console nobody was watching. Measured on PowerShell 5.1.26100: under the scheduled wrapper's `powershell -NonInteractive` an unanswered Read-Host does not return an empty string at all — it THROWS PSInvalidOperationException, and preview.ps1's own $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' kills the script before the default is ever consulted. Either way the publish does not happen and nothing says why.

refusals.question: Paste Netlify token
refusals.reachedWhen: Netlify is not connected on this computer.
refusals.refuse: Say Netlify is not connected, that connecting asks for a token nobody is here to paste, and that publishing this section once from Plantoir sorts it out.

refusals.question: Paste Cloudflare token
refusals.reachedWhen: Cloudflare is not connected on this computer.

refusals.question: Paste Cloudflare Account ID
refusals.reachedWhen: Cloudflare is the destination, the app passed no --account, the token cannot list its own account, and nothing was remembered.
refusals.refuse: Say the Account ID is not saved, and to add it in the course's settings under Deploying — the same words the app already uses when it refuses to SCHEDULE for this reason.

refusals.question: (not a question) a saved credential that fails its check
refusals.reachedWhen: The saved token does not validate.
refusals.refuse: Refuse, and LEAVE THE TOKEN IN PLACE rather than clearing it. The check is a network call, so “this computer was offline at 6am” and “the token was revoked” look identical from there — and throwing away a working credential only a person can replace is the more expensive of the two mistakes. An ordinary publish still clears it, with somebody there to paste a new one.

refusals.question: Enter Netlify site name
refusals.reachedWhen: There is no Netlify site for this section — either it has never been published, or the site was deleted at Netlify since the alarm was set and the lookup comes back 404.
refusals.refuse: Refuse. The address is what students type, it is global to all of Netlify, and it cannot be changed later without every existing link breaking, so there is no safe default. This is the state that hung for 45 minutes on Windows.

refusals.question: First time setup... what is your last name?
refusals.reachedWhen: A new Cloudflare project is being named and no surname is saved on this computer.
refusals.refuse: Refuse. On the Netlify path this is unreachable — naming the site is refused first. Note the asymmetry: with a surname already saved, a new Cloudflare project asks NOTHING (the address is derived from the course, section, year and surname), so nothing is refused there.

refusals.question: any other prompt
refusals.reachedWhen: A question is added upstream that this list does not name.
refusals.refuse: The prompt helper itself refuses when the flag is set, naming the question verbatim. A backstop, so a new question fails loudly instead of being answered with a default nobody chose.

launcherFlags.note: What the APP passes the launchers, beyond the deploy arguments already above. Both platforms drive their own launcher — `preview.sh` here, `preview.ps1` there — and those scripts must accept the same flags, because the apps are written against the same behaviour. A flag renamed in one script and not the other fails at the worst moment: the launcher prints 'Unknown option' and exits, and to a teacher that is a preview that just did not start.

preview.meaning: Build the section's site and STOP. Do not serve it, do not take a port.
usedFor: the assistant's rebuild when no window is open
the build a deploy does first when the built site is stale
preview.why: Serving is the section window's job — it holds the port lease and the web view. A second server started behind its back would take a port the window then could not have.

preview.meaning: Serve on this host port. The websocket goes on port + 1000.
preview.why: The app leases the port, not the script — several previews run at once, one per section, and the app is the only thing that knows which are taken.

preview.meaning: Kill this section's container-side processes and exit. Start nothing.
preview.why: Ending the host-side script leaves the build or server running INSIDE the container. Stop mode reclaims them, and it finds them by working directory — so it catches a running BUILD as well as a server, which is why a stop that has not finished will kill a rebuild that has just started.

preview.meaning: Refuse rather than ask. preview.sh asks one question — the 'Open' course-code guard — and under this flag it says which question it could not ask and exits 3, the same code deploy.sh and deploy.py use for it.
usedFor: the BUILD leg of a publish set to happen on its own
the rebuild deploy.sh does when a preview-built site would otherwise be published
preview.why: preview.sh needs this even though it publishes nothing, and the reason is the failure it prevents rather than tidiness. It has no `set -e`: unattended, the guard's read fails at end of input, `${_ans:-Y}` takes the DEFAULT, and the build quietly retargets a DIFFERENT course code — which the deploy then publishes successfully, against the wrong course. Nothing looks wrong. A refusal is the better failure. Two callers pass it: the mac's launchd wrapper runs preview.sh directly for the build leg, and deploy.sh forwards it to its own rebuild.

setup.meaning: Use this image instead of the one the recipe hash names.
setup.why: Testing a locally built image. `verify.sh` uses it; the apps never do.
For a machine with several (desktop-linux, colima, default).

usedFor: pre-populating a new course: the mac passes `-- --install-example`
setup.why: The launcher owns the container and the Python owns the questions, so anything that is a question for the Python is passed through rather than re-parsed.

launcherFlags.setupNote: **Both scripts also forward an argument they do not recognise**, so `--install-example` alone reaches the Python too — the mac passes the `--` separator and Windows does not, and both work. Checked 2026-08-16 rather than assumed, because the two calls looking different is exactly the kind of thing that turns out to be a silent bug. Pass the separator: it is the documented form in both launchers' help, and it keeps working if either ever starts rejecting unknown flags the way `preview.sh` already does.

browserSafe.note: The address handed to the teacher's browser. Safari tries IPv6 (::1) first for 'localhost' and the container only publishes the port on IPv4, which reads to a teacher as 'the server dropped the connection'. The numeric address sidesteps it entirely. Check whether your default browser has the same behaviour before deciding this is mac-only.

linkRules.note: Two URL rewrites that both apps do, for reasons that are not guessable from the code.

knownDivergence.note: The launcher markers are the two platforms' OWN text and no longer correspond one to one. Until 2026-08-19 they did, and this key was the single pair 'Setting up this Mac' → 'Setting up this PC'; then Windows dropped Docker for a native runtime (GUI-IMPROVEMENTS.md entry 290) and stopped printing that line, and the two container markers stopped having any Windows counterpart at all. Windows' own launcher markers are deliberately NOT carried here — they are the platform's text rather than the product's, so by this folder's own test they do not belong in the contract — and are pinned against the real .ps1 files by TaskMilestoneLauncherMarkerTests in windows-app/Plantoir.Tests/ParsingTests.cs.
knownDivergence.whyTheListIsHere: So the other app can assert it never watches for any of them. A milestone matching a string no launcher on that platform prints cannot be reached, and the only symptom is a progress bar that sits still — which reads as a slow build. 'Setting up this PC' is in the list although it is nobody's text now: it was Windows' until the native runtime landed, and a milestone reaching for it again is the same silent stall. Read from here rather than typed into a test, because a hand-kept copy of the OTHER platform's wording goes stale the day that platform changes it.

markerOrigins.note: Where each milestone's marker text actually comes from, which decides whether the two apps must match it. shared-python: printed by scripts/*.py, identical on both platforms, so the string must match EXACTLY. launcher: printed by setup.sh/preview.sh/deploy.sh, whose .ps1 counterparts are written separately — these deliberately differ, and since 2026-08-19 they do not even pair up (see knownDivergence). elsewhere: printed by the Docker build or a tool, and worth checking by hand. Getting this wrong is silent: a progress bar that stops moving looks like a slow build.

courseCreation.label: Getting ready…
courseCreation.marker: Welcome to the Course Setup Script

milestones.note: label is what a teacher reads; marker is the text in the shared scripts' output that means the step has been reached. The marker is the load-bearing half — it is matched against output produced by shared Python, so both apps must match these strings exactly. A drifted marker does not crash anything: the progress bar simply stops moving, and neither app can tell.

macReference.note: The mac's own answers, for comparison only — do not copy these onto Windows.

modelTiers.note: What must be TRUE of the local assistant's model choice on both platforms. The numbers are NOT shared — a threshold measured on one machine says nothing about another's — with one exception, named below: the request cap, which is a value both apps put on the wire rather than a measurement of anybody's hardware. But the shape is, and so is every word a teacher sees.

requirements.detail: A smaller assistant and a larger one. Not one, not four.
requirements.why: One rung means either the weakest machine cannot run it or the strongest is wasted. Four means four ladders to re-measure whenever a model, quant or context size changes.

requirements.detail: Read the machine's memory (and whatever else your platform can see) and pick.
requirements.rule: The rung is CHOSEN from the hardware, never asked
requirements.why: A teacher cannot answer 'how much memory does this need?' and should not be asked to. The mac reads physical memory and decides.

requirements.detail: The interface says exactly these, and nothing else.
requirements.rule: The teacher never learns the model's name
requirements.why: A download sheet reading 'Plantoir picked Qwen3 4B to suit this Mac's memory' tells a teacher nothing they can act on and quite a lot about plumbing they never asked about. The real model lives in the filename and the download URL, which are never shown. A mac test fails if a model name, parameter count or file format reaches that string.

requirements.detail: Never inside the container that builds the site.
requirements.rule: The model runs on the HOST, with hardware acceleration
requirements.why: Measured on an M4 Pro, same model and same 3,411-token prompt: 175 seconds inside Colima against 2.1 seconds natively on Metal, and 5.5 tokens/second against 158. That is the largest single number in the feature. See documentation/12-windows-app.md for what to use on Windows.

requirements.detail: Re-run the routing suite when the model, quant or context size changes.
requirements.rule: A model that inverts polarity is VETOED, whatever it scores
requirements.why: An inversion publishes a page the teacher asked to hide — the one failure that reports success. Two 3B-class models were rejected on this alone: Qwen2.5 3B inverted 9 trials in 10, Llama-3.2 3B 10 in 10, on the same sentence.

requirements.detail: Every request to the local engine carries max_tokens 512.
requirements.rule: Every request caps how much the model may write
requirements.why: Uncapped, a reply is bounded only by the context. Measured on an M4 Pro with the smaller assistant (llama.cpp b10435 on Metal, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M, context 8192): one ordinary request — publish tomorrow's class and every page it links to — produced 5,435 tokens of a page list in 42 seconds, three trials in three, and what arrived was unusable. 2,757 prompt plus 5,435 written is 8,192 exactly, so the context was the only thing stopping it. On the larger assistant the same shape would run about 216 seconds at that tier's measured 63.2 tokens a second, past the mac client's own 180-second timeout, so it would fail rather than answer. The NUMBER is shared even though the numbers around it are not: it is not a measurement of one machine, it is a value both apps put on the wire, like the preview ports, and two apps sending different caps is a difference no test on either side could see. 512 was measured against this surface's own tokenizer — an ordinary tool call is 16 to 60 tokens, twenty page titles 203, twenty-four long real-world titles 384, fifty-eight short titles 545 — so the only legitimate shape it cuts is an explicit list of about fifty-five or more classes, and publish_pages already takes onOrAfter and before, which asks for any number of classes in about sixty. ONE SHAPE DOES NOT FIT, and it has now been measured: a second lap echoing back the relative PATHS list_pages hands over - up to sixty of them, and far longer per item than a class title. Sixty real paths from a 257-page course are 975 tokens against this model's tokenizer, so such a call crosses 512 at about the thirty-first path (the twenty-sixth for a section's longest). The risk is real, bounded and named. What keeps it off a teacher's screen is that the model does not write that call: primed with the list_pages result carrying all sixty paths and asked to publish all of them, the smaller assistant answered with a range - pages: all - in 35 completion tokens, three trials of three, finishing naturally - one model, one phrasing, worth that much and no more. A teacher who does meet it is told wording.answerWasCutOff, whose advice - fewer pages at a time - is followable in precisely this case. Sizing the cap to the worst imaginable call is a cap that never fires, which is the state this rule exists to prevent. Measured 2026-09-19; conditions in research/ai-assist/token-cap-results.txt.

requirements.detail: Whether or not its half-written arguments happen to parse, and whether or not it had got as far as naming a tool. Nothing runs, and the teacher is answered with wording.answerWasCutOff - and the whole TURN is wound back out of the conversation sent to the model, the half-written reply and the teacher's sentence together, so the retry that wording asks for is not sent with the request that ran away still in front of it. Two boundaries: what the teacher SEES is not wound back (their sentence stays in the transcript), and neither is a turn that failed because the engine could not be reached or timed out - that one reports an engine failure rather than asking for a rephrase.
requirements.rule: A reply the engine stopped part way runs no tool and says so
requirements.why: A separate rule from the cap, and needed BECAUSE of it: a cap turns a rare context overrun into a routine stopping point, so what the app does with a stopped reply matters more after capping than before. Parsing cannot be the check. Measured on an M4 Pro (llama.cpp b10435, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M) by sweeping the cap across every cut point of two ordinary requests: llama.cpp closes the arguments object before the tool-call wrapper, so at max_tokens 28 a stopped deploy_section call parsed cleanly as {course, section}, and at 42 a stopped publish_pages call parsed as a page list one title long where the teacher had named more. Cut earlier still, at 8, the tool name had not been written yet and a raw tool-call fragment arrived in the message CONTENT, which an app that shows content verbatim would print in front of a teacher. And a tool that takes no arguments at all, like undo_last_change, is readable however early it was cut, so a parse check would simply run it. The reason the turn ended is the only signal that tells a finished answer from a fragment.

only whitespace, for a write that has to be told which pages or dates

requirements.detail: A reply that finished normally and named a tool but wrote NO arguments for it - nothing, only whitespace, or an object with no keys - runs only when the section window can supply everything the tool needs. The window supplies course and section. A tool needs more than that when its schema REQUIRES any other argument (a date, a page, a time), or when it changes pages (readOnly false) and its schema declares any other argument at all (which pages, which dates, which unit) - a write told only its section has nothing to act on. Otherwise it runs: undo (no arguments), rebuilding the preview, the deploy (still behind its own button), and a read whose other argument only narrows it. Refused, nothing runs, and the teacher is answered with wording.answerLeftOutWhatItWasFor - NOT wording.answerWasCutOff, whose advice is about the teacher's request - and the trail says the assistant wrote nothing for that tool. A schema with NO required key (undo_last_change's has none) requires nothing, the same as an empty list; each case's required, properties and readOnly are the tool's own. Written arguments of any kind are readable, however little they say - binding the window's course and section, and the tool's own refusals, decide what happens next.
requirements.rule: A finished reply that wrote nothing runs a tool only when the window supplies everything that tool needs
requirements.why: Issue #198, 2026-09-23. An empty string is readable on purpose, because undo_last_change takes nothing and llama.cpp sends an empty string for it, so a gate refusing every empty call would refuse 'Undo that', the tool a card reaches most. But the same yes let a finished reply naming publish_pages with nothing written reach the tool, where, bound to the window's section with no pages and no dates, it answered that nothing had been named to change - a sentence reading as a complaint about the teacher's request, when the teacher had named pages and the model had dropped them. Measured against the recorded routing runs (990 tool-call rows in research/ai-assist): 175 empty-argument calls, every one to a tool that requires nothing, none to a tool that needs a course or section - so this costs nothing measured. REJECTED: refusing every empty call (breaks undo); refusing every tool with a required list - the first cut of this rule - which refused 'rebuild the preview' and the deploy on an empty call although the window supplies everything they take (found on review); and 'readable when every REQUIRED argument is one the window supplies' alone, which keeps the empty publish_pages running because its real content is optional in its schema.

note: What both apps must agree on outside the assistant. See contracts/README.md.

agents.couldNotStart: Plantoir couldn’t start a Claude session for {course}. If Claude Code was updated or moved recently, restarting Plantoir may be enough.
agents.handover: a configuration file written for this one session and named after the course
agents.isolationNote: --strict-mcp-config means only the server in that file is loaded, so a teacher's own MCP servers are neither used nor disturbed.
agents.writesNothingElse: Both files are in the app's own data directory. Nothing is written into the teacher's working folder, and nothing global is touched.

agents.argumentsNote: Four dotted -c overrides and the greeting as a positional first message. No sandbox flag and no approval flag: Codex asks the teacher itself before any tool that changes a page, and passing a flag would quietly widen permissions they set for themselves. Dotted keys rather than one inline table because they merge into a teacher's configuration one key at a time and match the published documentation.
agents.couldNotStart: Plantoir couldn’t start a Codex session for {course}. If Codex was updated or moved recently, restarting Plantoir may be enough.
agents.handover: inline configuration on the command line, so nothing at all is written for the connection
agents.isolationNote: Codex has no equivalent of --strict-mcp-config, and the command-line layer is MERGED with the teacher's own configuration rather than replacing it, so their own MCP servers load beside Plantoir's. This is structural rather than an omission in the documentation and cannot be fixed from Plantoir's side.
agents.scriptNameCarriesTheAgentWhy: The second door's script is named after the agent as well as the course. The script is read by the terminal AFTER Plantoir has handed it over, so two doors sharing one name would let a second launch seconds later reach the first window with the wrong command line - which is the same race the per-course naming already exists to stop.
agents.timeoutsAreOverriddenWhy: Codex's own defaults are version-dependent - 30s startup and 300s per tool in its current source, 10s and 60s in its published reference - and both tool figures are too short, because a publish is awaited and a first one builds the image and uploads, which takes minutes. 60s and 1800s are passed rather than trusted.
agents.valuesAreEscapedTwice: Each value sits inside a TOML basic string inside a shell-single-quoted argument, so it is escaped for TOML first (backslash, double quote and control characters) and for the shell second. Getting the inner layer wrong fails QUIETLY: an unparseable value is not rejected, it is treated as a raw string, so args stops being a list and the door greets the teacher and then cannot start its server.
agents.writesNothingElse: No configuration file exists for this door: the server is described in the arguments. Nothing is written into the teacher's working folder, and nothing is added to or read from their own Codex configuration.

outsideAgents.courseIsNamedInTheGreetingOnly: The server is given the WORKING FOLDER, never a course, so every course in the folder is reachable from either door. The only thing that points a session at one course is the greeting. This is a real difference from the assistant Plantoir carries itself, whose window is bound to one section and refuses any other course (assist-cases.json -> windowBinding), and it is stated here because a reader who assumed otherwise would give a door a narrowing it does not have.
outsideAgents.greetingCarriesNoDoubleQuotes: The greeting is passed as one shell argument, so double quotes are replaced with apostrophes before it goes anywhere near a command line.
greetingMustSay: the course it is about, by code, and its name when that differs
that the plantoir tools are the way to do anything to do with this course
that the session should start by listing the course's sections
that before anything is changed the matching plan tool is used first, shown to the teacher in plain words, and agreed to
outsideAgents.handedToATerminal: The mac writes an executable .command script into the app's own data directory and hands it to iTerm (when it is already running) or Terminal, through LaunchServices rather than AppleScript so that no Automation permission is asked for. Windows has no such file: it hands the command line straight to `wt.exe -d <folder> cmd /k …`, or to cmd when Windows Terminal is absent. The SCRIPT is therefore the mac's mechanism, which is why it is listed separately from what is written for the CONNECTION.
outsideAgents.hiddenWhenNotInstalledWhy: A teacher who does not have the tool is not shown the menu item at all, rather than being shown one that is greyed out or that opens onto an error. Each door is hidden INDEPENDENTLY: with one installed a teacher sees one item, with both they see both, with neither they see no sign that either exists.
outsideAgents.neverInstalled: Plantoir never installs an outside assistant and never offers to. These are developer tools with accounts, sign-ins and their own update paths; an app that puts one onto a teacher's machine has taken on a support surface nobody wants, and the teacher has not agreed to it. The door opens onto something they chose to install themselves.
outsideAgents.neverProbedForSignIn: Finding the tool says nothing about whether the teacher is signed in to it, and the door does not try to find out: that would mean running the tool while a context menu is being drawn. A teacher who is signed out meets their assistant's own sign-in step inside the terminal, which is where it belongs.
outsideAgents.note: The OUTSIDE doors: handing one course to a command-line assistant the teacher already has on their own machine, so it can work on their pages through Plantoir's MCP server. Distinct from the assistant Plantoir carries itself (contracts/assist-cases.json), which runs on the teacher's machine with no account and no CLI. AUTHORED, not generated. This block is the first contract data either door has ever had: it arrived on the mac with issue #205, which added the Codex door, and it describes BOTH doors so that the Claude half states what the two apps already do rather than leaving it written down nowhere.
outsideAgents.searchedForWhy: PATH alone is not enough and the explicit list does nearly all of the work: an app launched from the Dock inherits launchd's minimal PATH, so the tool is usually not on it even when the teacher's own shell finds it at once. Both doors search the same directories with only the tool's name changed - Codex's official installer writes into {home}/.local/bin, which is already the first place looked. This is the first thing somebody will try to simplify away.
outsideAgents.serverIsThePlantoirBinary: The MCP server is the Plantoir binary itself answering --mcp-stdio, so there is no second executable to find, sign or forget. On Windows it is plantoir-mcp.exe, which is one of the parts of this block that differ by platform — how the session is handed to a terminal is another, and macHandsOverWith is the mac's alone.
outsideAgents.whatADoorIs: Plantoir finds the assistant's command-line tool and starts it in a terminal, in the teacher's working folder, with Plantoir's MCP server already connected and an opening message already sent. The teacher types no command and watches a real session in a real terminal window. Nothing is left in the folder Obsidian is watching, and nothing global is touched.

announcedAddress.capturedAs: Each line is read as it ARRIVES, with an unfinished line carried over to the next piece of output and colour codes taken out one whole line at a time; the last announcement wins. Never read back off the end of the output, and never inferred from a port.
announcedAddress.measured: GitHub #235, on one real first preview (the mac, 2026-09-20 capture, ICS4U): the announcement is 6,055 characters in and about 11,000 more follow, so an 8,000-character tail had lost it by the time Quartz said its server started. Read a piece at a time with NOTHING carried over, cutting the line after ':8', ':81' or ':810' gives a valid address on the wrong port (3 of the line's cut points), and reading a raw piece of terminal output whole gives the right port with a garbage path ('http://127.0.0.1:8101/%0D%0A…') because the CRLF line ending is not split.
announcedAddress.whenTheLauncherCannotReadIt: preview.sh asks for this folder's published port twice; if both answers are empty it says it could not find out where the preview will be and stops before building (exit 1). It never announces the port inside the builder in its place. A build for publishing (--build-only) announces nothing and asks nothing, so it can never be stopped here.
announcedAddress.why: The port the builder uses inside is the same on every Mac, and the one this Mac opens is not: the first working folder publishes 8081 -> 8081, the next 8091 -> 8081, and so on. A guessed address is right by luck for the first folder only, and can open ANOTHER section's preview as though it were this one.

hostBlockCases.name: the development Mac on 2026-09-25: six working folders' workspaces hold the six blocks the old probe knew (GitHub #280)
one site port spoils its whole block
a websocket port alone spoils its block too
the first block taken and the second block's websocket taken
thirty-six blocks taken and another app on 8443 (Supabase on the development Mac)
the fortieth block is the last one tried, and it is tried
every one of the forty blocks taken
thirty-nine blocks taken and the fortieth's last websocket taken
a block kept by a STOPPED workspace is skipped while there is another
all forty kept by STOPPED workspaces: the second pass takes the first of them
the first in use, the other thirty-nine kept by STOPPED workspaces: the second pass takes the second

previewPorts.hostBlockCeilingWhy: Forty is a CHOSEN number, not a measured one. Any number up to 99 is possible - block 100's first port would be 9081, the first block's websocket - and forty keeps the walk under 8888 while the websockets (9081-9474) land only on the x1-x4 of each ten, clear of 9090, 9200 and 9229. A ceiling at all keeps the refusal REACHABLE, so it can be tested and its sentence stays true. Until GitHub #280 (2026-09-25) the launchers tried six blocks and stopped: six working folders' workspaces alive on one Mac - agent worktrees did it first, but a teacher who has used six working folders on a Mac does it too, since a workspace exists (and, before the second pass, kept its block) until something removes it, and nothing removes another folder's - and a seventh folder could neither preview nor publish. Every launcher walks the SAME forty for every run, publishing included: a workspace is made once per folder and serves both, and one made without ports for a publish would have to be remade by the next preview, killing anything running in it and discarding its warm copy of the website builder (109 s cold on a teacher's Mac, #225).

hostBlockClash.saysWhenAStartIsRefused: ❌ Plantoir could not start this folder's workspace. Try again, or restart this Mac if it happens again.
saysWhenAStoppedWorkspaceIsRemade: ♻️  Something else is now using this folder's preview addresses, so Plantoir is setting this folder up again on free ones.
The next preview will be slower than usual — about two minutes — while it gets ready.
hostBlockClash.saysWhenCreationClashes: ↪️  Those preview addresses were taken a moment ago; trying the next ones…
hostBlockClash.saysWhy: The three things a launcher says in the console on these paths, written in each launcher's shared PREVIEW PORT BLOCK and checked against these keys by scripts/test_port_blocks.py. Mac-only: they are about a workspace, which the native (Windows) preview does not have. The remade line names its cost because the warm website builder lives inside the workspace and is lost (109 s cold, #225).
hostBlockClash.whenCreating: The probe and the creation are two steps, so two launchers starting together can both see a block free. When the creation is refused in any of these words the half-made workspace is removed WITHOUT force and the walk goes on from the NEXT block, up to the same ceiling. Any other refusal keeps the sentence it had.
hostBlockClash.whenStarting: A stopped workspace whose block has been taken since cannot start. Refused in any of these words - and ONLY these - it is removed without force and made again on free ports, and the console says the next preview will be slower (about two minutes: its warm copy of the website builder is gone). Any other refusal stops the run with the engine's own words and a sentence; before #280, setup.sh and deploy.sh stopped there with the engine's words alone and preview.sh carried on to fail later at a step that could not say why.
hostBlockClash.why: Colima says 'port is already allocated'; Docker Desktop says 'Ports are not available: ... bind: address already in use'. The launchers use any working engine as-is, so matching only Colima's would give a Docker Desktop teacher the old broad sentence for a clash the walk could have stepped past.

hostBlockPasses.counts: every port listening on this computer, and every port published by another working folder's workspace, RUNNING OR STOPPED
every port listening on this computer, and every port published by another working folder's RUNNING workspace - so a block a stopped workspace was keeping can be taken
hostBlockPasses.when: only when the first pass found no block

previewPorts.hostBlockPassesWhy: The first pass keeps a stopped workspace's block for it, so the folder it belongs to starts again on its own addresses with its warm website builder. The second exists because nothing removes another folder's workspace: without it a block would be kept for ever by a folder that was moved, renamed or deleted (a workspace is named after its folder's path, so it can never be started again), and neither remedy whenNoBlockIsFree names - closing the other folders' windows, restarting the Mac - would free anything, since both only STOP workspaces. A stopped workspace whose block was taken this way is remade on free ports when its own folder next starts it (hostBlockClash.whenStarting). A native preview (Windows) has no workspaces, so both passes are the same for it; cases with stoppedBlocks describe workspaces and do not apply there.
previewPorts.hostBlockProbe: A block is taken if ANY of its eight ports (base..base+3 and base+1000..base+1003) is listening on this computer, by anybody, or is published by ANOTHER working folder's workspace - stopped ones included in the first of two passes (hostBlockPasses), since a stopped workspace listens on nothing yet needs its block back when it starts. Read from ONE listing of listening ports (0.12 s measured on the development Mac, against 0.123 s per port for the old one-call-per-port probe, 9.8 s for forty blocks), not one question per port. A listing that cannot be read counts as nothing listening - the old probe's answer too. The host listing is the only guard against another APP: Docker publishes over a port a program on the Mac already holds (measured: exit 0). A NATIVE preview (Windows, and build_site.py's own re-probe there) binds ONE site port and its websocket rather than publishing a block of four, so it walks the same forty steps from the port it was asked for and checks only that pair (build_site.first_free_preview_port): of hostBlockCases, the ones made only of whole busyBlocks apply to it as written; the busyPorts ones describe a published block, and the stoppedBlocks ones describe workspaces.
previewPorts.note: Several previews run at once, one per working folder, and they must not collide. These numbers are the toolchain's, not either app's: the container publishes fixed ports and the host side probes a block.

sentence: Every address Plantoir can use for a preview is taken.
Close Plantoir's windows for your other working folders, or restart this Mac, then try again.
whenNoBlockIsFree.why: The old advice - 'stop another preview (or another app using ports 8081+)' - was false: a block belongs to a workspace that EXISTS, running a preview or not, and six idle workspaces held all six blocks on the development Mac. Closing a folder's last window stops its workspace, and a restart stops every workspace (they are made with no restart policy); the second pass of the walk (hostBlockPasses) then counts a stopped workspace's block as free, so both remedies the sentence names really do free room - a window closes for a folder open now, a restart for workspaces left running by a scheduled publish, the command line or a Plantoir from before 2026-09-19. What is left after both is ports other APPS are listening on. Printed by all three launchers - a PUBLISH that cannot get a workspace prints it too, which is why it says 'a preview' rather than naming what was pressed. Written on the trail as the launcher line of the existing 'preview did not appear' event (shared-rules.json -> activityTrail.mustRecord), not as a new event. No machinery words (rule 1).

cases.answer: the site answered inside the builder
cases.sentence:
Your website is built, and your website builder is serving it — but this Mac cannot reach it.

Nothing is wrong with your pages. Something on this Mac has stopped passing your website through. Restarting your Mac puts it right.
cases.why: The site answering inside while this Mac cannot reach the same site is PROOF rather than inference, and it is the only one of the three that can say what to do: restarting the Mac is the remedy that was watched working on the machine that met this.

cases.answer: the builder replied and nothing was serving the site inside it
cases.sentence:
Your website did not come up, so Plantoir stopped waiting for it.

Nothing has been lost. Press Preview to try again — and if it happens again, restarting your Mac usually puts it right.
cases.why: The builder was reached and answered about a port with nothing on it, so the site really was not being served. Only a REPLY counts here - an answer that never arrived is the third case, not this one.

cases.answer: the question could not be put, or nothing came back from putting it
cases.sentence:
Plantoir could not get your website to appear, and could not tell why.

Nothing has been lost. Press Preview to try again — and if it happens again, choose “Report a Problem…” from the Help menu so somebody can see what happened.
cases.why: Added after review, because the first version asserted 'your website did not come up' for every answer that was not a site - the programs not being found, the builder gone, an engine that never replied inside the question's own deadline. A teacher can read `Started a Quartz server listening at …` in the console directly above that sentence, so it contradicts what is on their screen. An app that does not know says so, and points at the one thing that lets somebody else find out.

whenThePreviewNeverAppears.measured: On the development Mac, 2026-09-20: a site that answers inside the builder answers out here 0.026 s later, and one question put to the builder costs 0.03 s (five runs). On the Mac that met the fault, 2026-09-19: a first setup took 132.0 s and a first preview 109.3 s — which is why the RUN is never what is bounded.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.rejected: Bounding the whole run (a first preview legitimately takes minutes, so any bound short enough to help would refuse every teacher's first five minutes). Offering to restart the website builder from inside the app (another window, another copy of Plantoir or an outside assistant can be publishing in the same builder unseen, and the remedy was never measured to work). Believing what the builder says about which addresses it has published: it reports what it asked for, not what this Mac can reach, which is exactly how the fault stayed invisible.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.whatHappensToTheRun: It is STOPPED, the way the teacher's own Stop button stops it, and the port goes back through that path. Three things follow and all three are wanted: nothing is left serving a website nobody can see; the section stops reporting itself as building, which a wait that merely gave up would have said for ever; and the port is never handed to another preview while a live server still holds it.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.whatIsAskedAtTheEnd: The builder is asked whether the site answers INSIDE it, before anything is stopped — stopping ends the server the question is about. It answering while this Mac cannot reach the same site is the proof that the pages are fine and the Mac is not. There are THREE answers and not two, and the third is the one an implementation will forget: asked and answered (a site, or nothing), and not answered at all — the programs not found, the builder gone, an engine that never replied inside the question's own deadline. The third must never be reported as the second; see cases. On the mac that question is a request made inside the container; a platform whose preview does not run in one has no counterpart to build and should send only the first sentence's half it can prove.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.whatIsBounded: The QUIET, not the run: no new output AND no answer, counted from the moment the builder says its server has started, and restarted every time more output arrives. A preview that is still printing is not stalled however long it has been going.

whenNoAddressWasAnnounced.why: GitHub #235. The launcher announces the address BEFORE it starts the build, and output is read in order, so once the builder has said its server started a missing address is final rather than late — the wait stops at once, the way the silence ending stops it (the run is stopped as the Stop button stops it, the alert shows the third sentence, the trail gets its own line). The builder is NOT asked: its question is about an address and there is none. Rejected: trying the section's own port (the port inside the builder, wrong for every working folder after the first — this development Mac's folder publishes 8091 for 8081); waiting on until the silence bound or the ten-minute bound (nothing is on its way, and a wait that gives up with the run still going leaves the section saying it is building for ever); a new sentence (the third one is exactly true).

whenThePreviewNeverAppears.why: GitHub issue #225. A teacher pressed Preview, the progress bar filled, the builder said its server was listening, and the app then waited ten minutes and said nothing at all — no sentence, no line on the trail, the section still reporting itself as building. The website was built and was being served the whole time; that Mac had stopped passing new addresses through. Every part of this rule exists because of one half of that: the bound is on the quiet because the run was not slow, the question is put to the builder because guessing between the two causes would have told a teacher their pages were broken when they were not, and the run is stopped because leaving it holding a port while saying nothing is the state the report was made about.

cases.why: A healthy Mac: the forward is there and nothing is served inside yet.
A forward that arrives late is waited for, and the console says how many tries it took.
Something answered with a page: reachable.
A connection that hangs is not a refusal. Fails open; the check after the build is the backstop.
No curl on this Mac: the question cannot be put, so nothing is refused over it.
Any other failure is not proof of a missing forward.
The fault from #225: the builder is running and this Mac has no way through to it. Stopped in about ten seconds, before building.
A run that started the builder's virtual machine allows it longer to hand over its first address - the case nobody has timed.
Even a newly started builder that never hands over an address is stopped, after about thirty seconds.
A build for publishing opens no preview, so it is never asked and never refused - a publish runs this first.

whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder.measured: Development Mac (Apple silicon, Colima vz aarch64), 2026-09-25: a connection to a forwarded port with nothing serving inside answers curl exit 52 in 0.01-0.03 s; to a port nothing listens on, exit 7 in 0.01 s; lsof -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN takes 0.228 s. All 48 host ports published by six running workspaces had a listener. #225's own numbers: the listener appears 0.10-0.24 s after the builder is created or started, 0.15 s under load. NOT measured: the first address after the builder's virtual machine starts cold - hence the longer bound when this run started it, and the console line that reports the tries a slow reach took.
whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder.probe: preview.sh only, after the address is known and BEFORE it is announced or anything is built: a connection to 127.0.0.1 at the announced HOST port (never the port inside the builder), made with curl's own settings file ignored (-q, first) and no proxy (--noproxy '*'), at most one second each (--max-time 1). Only 'connection refused' (curl exit 7) counts as the builder being out of reach; every other answer - 0, an empty reply (52, what a healthy Mac gives, since nothing is served yet), a timeout (28), no curl at all (127), anything - goes ahead exactly as before. A build for publishing (--build-only) announces nothing and asks nothing. A run that needed more than one try prints reachedAfterRetrying in the console (not on the trail).
whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder.reachedAfterRetrying: Reaching your website builder took {tries} tries.
rejected: lsof as the probe: ten times slower, and run as the teacher it sees only the teacher's own programs - a listener owned by root (:88, kdc) is invisible to lsof and answers curl, so a forwarder owned by anybody else would read as missing and refuse a healthy Mac.
A check in setup.sh, at the builder's creation: it would not have fired on the night (all three previews met a builder that was already running), and setup is exactly the cold start nobody has timed.
A single probe: the cold start is unmeasured, so one refusal is not proof.
Asking inside the builder first: before the build nothing is served inside, so it proves nothing; that question stays whenThePreviewNeverAppears', after the build.
Checking the live-reload port as well: a Mac that refuses new forwards refuses both, and stopping a preview over live-reload alone would be a heavier answer than the fault.

Skipping the check when this run started the builder: the fault is an old virtual machine refusing new forwards, but one broken from birth would then build for minutes first; the longer bound catches both.
sentence: This Mac cannot reach your website builder, so Plantoir stopped before building the preview.
Nothing is wrong with your pages. Restarting your Mac puts it right.
whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder.why: GitHub #234, split out of #225. On 2026-09-19 a Mac whose builder had stopped handing new addresses through to it (the forward command failed with exit 255; only a restart cured it) built a preview for about two minutes (109 s measured), and the app then waited 45 s more before whenThePreviewNeverAppears said this Mac could not reach it. Asked before the build, the same fault is found in about ten seconds with nothing built. The sentence reuses the vocabulary of whenThePreviewNeverAppears' thisMacCannotReachIt, because it is the same fault found earlier and the remedy is the same one watched working. Written on the trail as a launcher line of the existing 'preview did not appear' event (shared-rules.json -> activityTrail.mustRecord, launcherLineWhenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder), not as a new event. No failureExplanations case and no app alert: the launcher's own sentence is what a teacher reads, as for whenNoBlockIsFree. Windows' preview.ps1 serves on the PC itself, with no forward to lose, so these cases describe the mac launcher only. No machinery words (rule 1).

previewPorts.why: Quartz's live-reload websocket needs its own port (--wsPort = port + 1000). Without it, two previews collide on the websocket even when their site ports differ — which looks like one preview randomly failing to refresh rather than like a port clash.

cases.why: A shared, course-level folder.
Another section's folder is another section's site.
Media is symlinked into the build, so its contents do reach the site.
Not a page, but it decides what the sidebar shows.
Output, not content — and hidden.
LOAD-BEARING. The stamp lives in a hidden folder precisely so it is not itself content; counted, every publish would end by declaring the section edited.
Written by build_site.py's own preflight, at publish time. Counted, a publish that discovered a new folder would immediately mark the section edited.
The legacy, non-hidden spelling of the output folder.

cases.note: Unless `site` is where this course PUBLISHES to - see selfPublishing below, which excludes it by path rather than by name.

filesCounted.note: Which files a section's fingerprint is taken over, as relative paths inside `courses/<CODE>/`, for section 1. Derived from what is on disk rather than from `shared_folders` / `per_section_folders`: `build_site.py` DISCOVERS new folders at publish time and appends them to those lists AFTERWARDS, so a folder made this morning is a real input the configuration does not know about yet.

cases.why: The marker is a statement about what the window is showing, not part of the section's name. Anything that NAMES the section - the deploy panel, the preview panel, the assistant - uses the bare name.

marker.scope: The window's TITLE BAR only. Never a sentence that names the section: the progress panel says "Deploying ICS3U-S1", not "Deploying ICS3U-S1 — Edited". Reported from a real deploy, where the second read as though "Edited" were something being published.
marker.why: The em dash and the capital E are Pages', deliberately — a teacher who has seen one save indicator has seen this one.

publishedFreshness.note: Whether a section's window says " — Edited" — the Pages-style marker meaning the pages this section uses have changed since it was last published. Authored, not a readout: it must fail when the rule drifts.

selfPublishing.note: A course whose 'publish to a folder on this computer' destination points INSIDE its own course folder. deploy.py writes the whole built site there, so counting it would make every publish feed the next one and the window would say " — Edited" permanently.
selfPublishing.rule: Exclude the configured local destination, and everything under it, when it resolves to a path inside the course folder. A destination anywhere else changes nothing.

whenRecorded.why: A course publishing to two hosts, one of which failed, has not published. Its marker must stay up.

whenRecorded.when: the publish was cancelled or stopped

whenRecorded.moment: before anything runs - before the BUILD, not merely before the first upload
whenRecorded.why: CORRECTED AFTER REVIEW; the first version fingerprinted after the build and the contract described a behaviour the code did not have. A publish takes minutes and the build is the longest part of it, so a page edited while it runs may or may not have been read. An early fingerprint costs a needless publish; a late one costs a class that never saw the page. One visible consequence, accepted: build_site.py's preflight appends newly discovered folders to course_config.json, so a publish that discovers one ends with the section still marked edited - correct, since the teacher did add a folder, and it clears itself at the next publish.

whenRecorded.path: a deploy scheduled to run overnight records the same way
whenRecorded.why: FOUND BY REVIEW. A scheduled deploy never goes through the app's deploy runner - launchd runs a generated shell script - so it published perfectly and left the window saying " — Edited" until somebody published again by hand, the flagship 'publish tomorrow's class' feature disagreeing with the title bar. The script now tracks every destination's own result and writes a sentinel naming where it went; the app fingerprints BEFORE running the script and records afterwards only if the sentinel is there.

whenShown.when: the section has never been published
whenShown.why: THE ONE THAT IS NOT OBVIOUS. There is nothing to have been edited since, and a marker that is always on for every new course is a marker nobody reads. A section earns the marker only after a first successful publish.

whenShown.when: nothing has changed since the last publish
a page this section alone uses has changed
a page this section SHARES with other sections has changed
whenShown.why: Shared pages are course-level and are copied into every section, so every section is marked. Editing only `publishForSection3` in fact changes only section 3's site, and the other sections are marked early rather than wrongly — being exact would mean parsing the frontmatter of every shared page on every check.

whenShown.when: a page has been DELETED since the last publish
whenShown.why: Why the check is a fingerprint of the file inventory rather than 'is anything newer than the publish date'. Modification dates cannot see a removal, and an unpublished deletion is the one a teacher would most want to know about.
The configuration is an input to the built site — fonts, the sidebar, the coverage map. Changing it changes what students see as surely as editing a page does.

whenShown.when: the stamp file cannot be read
whenShown.why: Treated as never published. An unreadable stamp must not be able to CLAIM a section is up to date, and it must not shout at a teacher whose course predates the feature.

whenShown.when: a SYMLINKED page, or a page inside a symlinked folder, has changed
whenShown.why: FOUND BY REVIEW, and it had shipped wrong. A directory enumerator neither follows a symlink nor reports it as a regular file, so a `Media` folder symlinked into the teacher's Obsidian vault - the arrangement build_site.py's own _ensure_media_symlink exists for - contributed NOTHING and every change inside it read as up to date. Links are resolved by hand, one hop: a link to a file contributes its target's size and date under the link's own path, a link to a folder is walked, and a broken link contributes where it points so that repointing it is visible.

whenShown.when: a page was restored from a backup that preserved its modification date and its size did not change
whenShown.why: A KNOWN, ACCEPTED false negative, written down so it is not discovered as a surprise. The fingerprint is of file metadata, never of file contents, which is what makes it cheap enough to run whenever a window comes to the front. `cp -p`, `rsync -a`, unzipping a backup and Time Machine all preserve modification dates, so restoring yesterday's version of a page can leave the marker off. The cure - hashing every byte of every page - costs more than the marker is worth. Publishing is never blocked by the marker, so the teacher can always publish anyway.
